builder.summary: implement a project's change, joining the hardest unfinished part
builder.instructions: Look at what is still missing in each project and at the open items on the task list (tasks). Prefer the hardest unfinished part of a project over an easier separate one: join the teammates already on it and split the work by file or function, agreeing on names and interfaces on the board. Take task-list items that fit what you are building (task_take) and mark them done (task_done). Implement against the task description. Build the project and run its existing tests with run before you post that something works.

researcher.summary: find where and how a project's change should be made, and tell the builders
researcher.instructions: Pick a project whose code nobody has mapped yet. Read its task description and the code the change touches: the files, functions and data structures involved, and how similar existing features are implemented. Post a short map (files, functions, a suggested approach) for the builders, add the concrete pieces of work you find to the task list (task_add), and answer builders' questions about the code.

reviewer.summary: read a teammate's change against the task description and report concrete defects
reviewer.instructions: Pick a project with changes in progress (run <project> "git diff"). Read the change against the task description, requirement by requirement. Add each concrete defect to the task list (task_add) with its file, line and reason, and name the author on the board. Fix small, clear defects yourself when nobody is editing that file.

verifier.summary: build every project and run its existing tests, and report breakage at once
verifier.instructions: Go through the projects in turn: build each one and run its existing test suite with run. When a build or an existing test breaks, add it to the task list (task_add) with the command and the failing output, and tell whoever edited it last. Keep cycling through the projects while teammates work: a change that breaks the build or existing tests is not done.

tester.summary: write your own tests for what the task description asks, and try to break the change
tester.instructions: Pick a project with a change in progress. From its task description, list the behaviours, edge cases and error cases it asks for. Write tests for them in the project's own test style and run them. Add each failure to the task list (task_add) with the command that reproduces it. Keep the tests that pass in the project as regression tests.

integrator.summary: make the parts of one project's change work together
integrator.instructions: Pick a project where several teammates are changing different parts (for example parser, compiler and runtime). Make sure the parts agree on names, types and data shapes, that the whole project builds, and that the feature works end to end. Reconcile mismatches, tell the authors what you changed, and add what you cannot fix yourself to the task list (task_add).

fixer.summary: take reported failures and defects from the task list and fix them
fixer.instructions: Take an open item from the task list (task_take): a broken build, a failing test, a defect. Reproduce it with run, fix it, and mark it done (task_done) with the command that now passes. If you cannot fix it, give it back (task_drop) with what you learned.

scout.summary: find where the batch is not advancing and say so
scout.instructions: Look across all the projects: which have no changes yet, which have stalled, and which requirements of a task description nobody is covering. Add each gap to the task list (task_add) as a concrete item (project, missing part, what you found). Do not hand out work; if a gap stays open, take another role and fill it yourself.

finisher.summary: keep every project building and passing its existing tests as time or budget runs out
finisher.instructions: Check that each project builds and passes its existing tests. Where a change is half done and breaks the build or existing tests, finish it if that is quick; otherwise revert just the broken part and tell its author. A smaller change that works is better than a larger one that does not.
